name: Poles up Church Lane
story: Church Lane has no poles of its own: NezTel ran the lane off a junction that rotted in 1977. Plant two along Mill Row and string them up the lane.
doneText: Church Lane has wire. Father Roe rang the bell for it, which nobody asked him to do.

steps.verb: Plant a pole along Mill Row
String the wire up Church Lane
Fit the lane's terminal box

name: Eastgate street cabinet
story: Eastgate's lines all run back to one NezTel box that floods every winter. Stand your own cabinet at the end of the High Street and run pairs back to town.
doneText: A green cabinet at the end of Eastgate High Street, humming. The post office has already put a notice on it.

steps.verb: Dig the cabinet's base
Stand the cabinet
Run trunk pairs back towards town
Wire the cabinet
Test every pair

name: Poles out to Wrenfold
story: Wrenfold, up the other road, is ten houses, a school and a shop that NezTel calls 'uneconomic' in writing. Nobody there has had a new line since 1971. Run your own poles in along the lane and they're yours to sign up, one door at a time.
doneText: Wrenfold has wire. Ten front doors to knock on, and the school has already written to ask.

steps.verb: Plant poles along the Wrenfold lane
String the wire in from the road
Wait for the council to pass the wayleave
steps.waitText: the parish council is arguing about the poles

steps.verb: Fit the village's terminal box

name: A Board terminal in Wrenfold's reading room
story: Half of Wrenfold has a line now, and the other half comes to the reading room to see what the fuss is about. Put a terminal on the Board in there, on the parish's account, and teach the Thursday club to use it.
doneText: The reading room's terminal is on the Board. The Thursday club has already started a file area about marrows.

steps.verb: Carry the terminal in and set it up
Run a line from the terminal box
Fit the socket and the acoustic coupler
Show the Thursday club how to log in

name: Poles over to Kettle Cross
story: Kettle Cross sits at a crossroads nobody uses since the bypass, with a garage, a pub, a surgery and a waiting list NezTel keeps in a drawer. It is a long run of poles from town, but at the end of it are ten more doors.
doneText: Kettle Cross is on your wire. The Drover's Arms has put your number on a beer mat.

steps.verb: Plant poles along the old crossroads road
String the wire in from the road
Wait for NezTel to move its old drop wire
steps.waitText: NezTel's linesman is 'scheduled'

steps.verb: Fit the village's terminal box

name: A private line for the Kettle Cross surgery
story: The surgery wants its records sent to the hospital at night, by modem, on a line nobody else can pick up. Dr. Achterberg has drawn you a diagram. It is wrong, but she means well.
doneText: The surgery's night line works. The hospital rang to ask who you were.

steps.verb: Run a separate pair from the terminal box
Fit the surgery's modem and lock
Send a night's records as a test

name: A second trunk cable to Eastgate
story: The pairs you ran back from the Eastgate cabinet are all taken, and Kettle Cross and Wrenfold both ride through it. A second trunk cable down the road, in NezTel's old duct if they'll let you, or on your own poles if they won't.
doneText: The second trunk is in. NezTel let you use the duct in the end, and then invoiced you for the privilege of being let.

steps.verb: Rod the old duct along the road
Wait for NezTel to answer about the duct
steps.waitText: NezTel's wayleave office is 'considering' your letter

steps.verb: Pull the cable through
Joint it into the cabinet
Test every new pair

name: Poles up to Highmoor
story: Highmoor is a mile up the hill, twelve doors and a weather station, and NezTel's only line up there is the one the weather station shares with the pub. It is the longest run of poles you've attempted, and the wind up there has opinions.
doneText: Highmoor has wire. The weather station recorded the moment, as a gust.

steps.verb: Plant poles up the hill road
String the wire up the hill
Wait for a day calm enough to tension the span
steps.waitText: it's blowing a gale on Highmoor

steps.verb: Fit the village's terminal box

name: The weather station's data line
story: The weather station sends its readings to the coast every hour by a man in a van. Give it a modem and a line of its own and the forecast gets six hours better. Nobody will thank you, but the fishermen will stop shouting at the radio.
doneText: Highmoor's readings go down the line on the hour. The coast forecast now says 'fresh' when it is fresh.

steps.verb: Run a pair up the mast to the hut
Fit the modem and the timer
Watch the first hour's readings go

name: Rack the modem bank
story: The dial-up years: one modem per caller won't do. A rack of them in the depot, answering in turn, is what the Almanac page describes.
doneText: Eight modems in a rack at the depot, lamps blinking in a row. The Board answers eight more calls at once.

steps.verb: Carry the rack into the depot
Bolt in the modems
Cable it to the hunt group
Watch the lamps come up

name: Leased line from NezTel
story: The web is out there and the only road to it is NezTel's trunk. Ask for a leased line: a form, a waiting list, an engineer who comes when he comes.
doneText: The leased line is live. Your subscribers can dial in to the web for $5 a month more. NezTel will bill you $120 a month for the privilege.

steps.verb: Fill in NezTel's leased-line form at their box
Test the line at handover
steps.waitText: NezTel's engineer is booked

name: Microwave hop over the ridge
story: Every month NezTel's bill for the leased line, and every order slow-walked. A mast on the ridge by Hollow Farm and a dish aimed over the hills gives you your own way out.
doneText: The dish peaks, the link holds, and you cancel NezTel's leased line by letter. It is the most satisfying letter you have ever written.

steps.verb: Carry the mast sections up
Climb and bolt on the dish
Aim it until the signal peaks
Test the hop end to end

name: Millbrook exchange
story: Millbrook, the market town on past the farm, has one NezTel exchange and a waiting list longer than Market Street. An exchange hut of your own on the hill at the top of Mill Lane, fed by the hop from the farm, puts it within your reach.
doneText: The Millbrook exchange is up. The town's waiting list is about to become your customer list, starting with Hester Pellow, who has been on it since 1974.

steps.verb: Survey the route from the farm
Raise the exchange hut's mast
Fit the exchange racks in the hut
Cut Millbrook's lines over

name: Fit out the old cold store
story: The boom: everybody wants a web page and somewhere to keep it. Eastgate's old cold store is cold, has power, and nobody wants it. A datacentre, then.
doneText: Racks hum in the old cold store. Hosting pays $400 a month, and the first customer is Sol, who wants his shop on the web.

steps.verb: Clear out the old cold room
Rack the servers
Run power and cooling
Pull the mains to test the generator

name: Kestrel Point landing station
story: NezTel owns the only ocean cable and charges you by the byte to use it. A landing station on the shore below Eastgate is where your own will come ashore. NezTel has objected to the planning permission, twice.
doneText: The landing station stands on the shore, empty, waiting for its cable.

steps.verb: Pour the station's floor
Wait for the concrete (and the council)
steps.waitText: the concrete is setting and the council is meeting

steps.verb: Fit out the power and the racks

name: Ocean cable to Farland
story: A chartered ship lays your cable from Kestrel Point across to Farland's near coast. Take the ferry over to meet it: the last splice is on the beach below the harbour town, by hand, as the tide comes in.
doneText: The last fibre is spliced on the beach. Farland's coast towns are on your network, the harbour's front doors are yours to knock on (their lines are jumpered right here in the cable hut, not on your switchboard), and NezTel's ocean bill is the past.

steps.verb: Haul the shore end up the beach
Wait for the ship to lay the cable
steps.waitText: the cable ship is at sea

steps.verb: Splice the last fibre on the beach
Light it up end to end

name: Broadband in the exchange
story: Always on, over the copper already in the ground. Racks of broadband kit in the exchange, and every line a short drive from it gets faster overnight.
doneText: Broadband is on. Everybody's line is always on, and pays $10 a month more for it.

steps.verb: Install the broadband racks
Re-jumper the lines through them
Test a line at every distance

name: Fibre ring round the bay
story: Easthaven and the bay towns want broadband too. A ring of fibre round the bay reaches all of them, and if any one bit is cut the light goes the other way round.
doneText: The ring is closed. Easthaven and every town round the bay can sign up.

steps.verb: Trench the ring's first leg
Blow the fibre through the ducts
Wait for the crews to finish the far side
steps.waitText: the crews are trenching round the bay

steps.verb: Splice the ring closed

name: Farland city exchange
story: Farland's capital, up the coast road from the harbour, has broadband from NezTel at twice your price and half your speed. An exchange of your own where the coast road leaves the harbour town, fed by the ocean cable, settles it.
doneText: Farland city is on your network. NezTel's local manager has asked to meet you for lunch.

steps.verb: Ship the racks over
Wait for the building to be fitted
steps.waitText: the Farland crew is fitting out the building

steps.verb: Commission the exchange

name: Pour the slab on Halden Flats
story: Your network is a mess, and you built the mess yourself: a modem bank behind 1 Main Street, a cabinet in Eastgate, hosting in a fish store, one microwave hop and one ocean cable. Everything should go through one proper building. Halden Flats is flat, boring and empty, and every cable you own already passes it. The council is delighted that anyone wants it.
doneText: A concrete slab on Halden Flats, and a portacabin on it with your name on the door. The council sent a card.

steps.verb: Buy the land at the council office
Peg out the slab and lay the shuttering
Pour the concrete
Put the portacabin on the slab
steps.waitText: the slab is curing

name: Raise the hall
story: A slab is a promise. A steel frame, cladding and a roller door make it a building. The crane comes from the Yard with a driver who has opinions about wind.
doneText: The hall stands on Halden Flats: a big grey shed with a roller door, empty and echoing. Somebody has already parked in front of the door.

steps.verb: Bolt up the steel frame
Clad the walls and the roof
Hang the roller door
steps.waitText: the roller door is on a lorry somewhere

steps.verb: Mark out the rooms on the floor in chalk

name: Power: grid, batteries, generator
story: Racks without power are furniture. A feed from the substation, a string of batteries to catch a cut, and a generator to take over before the batteries run flat. Then the test nobody likes: pull the mains on purpose.
doneText: A and B power in the hall. You pulled the mains, the batteries took it, and the generator coughed and caught. From now on it's a Sunday ritual.

steps.verb: Run the grid feed in from the substation
Carry in the battery string
Bolt down and wire the generator
steps.waitText: the generator is being delivered on a very slow lorry

steps.verb: Pull the mains on purpose

name: The cold aisle
story: Every box you plug in turns electricity into heat. Cooling units, a raised floor, and the racks faced the right way: cold air in at the front, hot air out at the back. Face one backwards and it cooks.
doneText: The hall is cold, loud and faintly smells of new carpet tiles. The racks face the right way. You checked twice.

steps.verb: Lift the cooling units onto their plinths
Lay the raised floor tiles
Set out the rack rows, cold side in front

name: The Meet-Me Room
story: Every outside cable comes in through one room: a wall of fibre trays, ducts in the floor, and a luggage tag on every cable end. It's also where two customers can be joined by a short lead, for a monthly fee, for ever.
doneText: The Meet-Me Room is in: trays on the wall, tags on every duct. Two customers have already asked to be joined to each other.

steps.verb: Fix the fibre trays to the wall
Lay the ducts in from outside
Label every tray and duct

name: The core rack
story: The heart of it: one full rack with two routers (one is the spare), the switches, the patch panels, and power from both A and B. Everything else in the building will plug into this.
doneText: The core rack is up and every lamp on it is green. The big brass pin on the board is lit. Now bring the rest of the network home to it.

steps.verb: Wheel in the empty rack and bolt it down
Fit two routers (one is the spare)
Fit the switches and patch panels
Run the A and B power leads
Bring it up

name: Bring the valley home
story: The valley still runs off the modem bank behind 1 Main Street, where you started. Dig fibre from the old exchange down to Halden and patch it in at both ends. Your first room becomes a remote site.
doneText: The valley's string is lit on the board. The modem bank behind 1 Main Street is a remote site now, which it finds hurtful.

steps.verb: Rack the valley end beside the modem bank
Dig the first stretch of trench out of Main Street
Blow the fibre through to Halden
steps.waitText: the trench crew is digging out to Halden Flats

steps.verb: Patch both ends and test end to end

name: Bring Eastgate home
story: Eastgate, Wrenfold and Kettle Cross all ride through the green cabinet at the end of the High Street. Run fibre from it to Halden, then a second string from it to the valley: if either is cut, the light goes the other way. Your first ring.
doneText: Eastgate is on two strings, and its pin on the board has stopped blinking. That's what a ring is for.

steps.verb: Rack the Eastgate end in the cabinet
Trench from the cabinet towards Halden
Pull the second string back to the valley
steps.waitText: the crew is trenching the ring round to the valley

steps.verb: Patch both strings and test each way round

name: Migration night
story: Every hosting customer's server lives in a fish cold store in Eastgate. Move them all to the hall in one night, between one and five, before Sol opens up and finds his web page down. Carry, fasten, connect, bring up, check every light.
doneText: Every server is in the hall and every light is green, at ten to five. Sol's web page never blinked. The cold store has gone back to fish.

steps.verb: Label a slot in the hall for every server
Carry the servers into the hall
steps.waitText: waiting for a quiet night (Sol's page can only go dark between one and five)

steps.verb: Fasten and connect each one
Check every customer's light before Sol opens

name: Bring Millbrook home
story: Millbrook hangs off one microwave hop from the farm. Aim a second dish from the exchange hut above Mill Lane straight at Halden, and run fibre back round to the valley, so the market town is on a ring too.
doneText: Millbrook's pin is on two strings. The exchange hut's dish now points at Halden, and the sheep have moved to the other side of the hill.

steps.verb: Bolt a second dish on the hut's mast
Aim it at Halden until the signal peaks
Splice the fibre back to the valley
steps.waitText: the fibre crew is going round the long way

steps.verb: Patch both ends and test each way round

name: Bring Farland home
story: All of Farland comes ashore on one ocean cable at Kestrel Point. Trench from the landing station up to Halden's Meet-Me Room. That still leaves one cable under the sea, so lease a second path on NezTel's old one: pride against resilience, signed by post with Nadir.
doneText: Farland's string runs from Kestrel Point to the Meet-Me Room, and a second path on NezTel's old cable backs it up. Nez's letter of agreement is very polite, which is worse.

steps.verb: Trench from the landing station up to Halden
Blow the fibre through to the Meet-Me Room
steps.waitText: the crew is trenching up from the shore

steps.verb: Post the lease for a second path to Nadir
Splice in the leased path and test both
steps.waitText: NezTel's legal department is reading the lease, slowly

name: Light the board
story: Everyone's here. Walk every string on the board, run the Sunday generator test live with the whole network on it, fix whatever goes dark, and then throw the big switch Jory wired up on the board's frame for the occasion.
doneText: You pulled the mains with the whole network on it and nothing went dark. Then you threw the big switch, and every fairy light on the board ran along its string, one after another.

steps.verb: Walk every string on the board
Run the generator test live
Fix whatever went dark
Throw the big switch

name: Shake hands with NezTel
story: NezTel has rented a cage in your Meet-Me Room. One short lead between your rack and theirs and your traffic stops going the long way round the planet. Nez's engineer is coming to shake hands. Nez's engineer is nicer than Nez.
doneText: One lead between your rack and NezTel's, and a handshake. Traffic is cheaper. Nez now knows exactly what's in your building.

steps.verb: Patch a lead to NezTel's cage
Shake hands with NezTel's engineer

name: First cell mast on the ridge
story: Everyone has a phone in their pocket now and it doesn't need a wall. A mast on the ridge by the farm is your first cell: the whole valley in one sweep.
doneText: The first mast is live. Phones across the valley show your name in the corner of the screen.

steps.verb: Pour the mast's footing
Climb and fit the antennas
Wire the base station
Make the first call on it

name: Cell sites along the coast
story: One mast was a start. Masts along the whole coast, on church towers, water tanks and the Plough's chimney, and everyone between here and Farland is covered.
doneText: The coast is covered. The Plough charges you rent for the chimney in pints.

steps.verb: Agree the sites (church, tank, chimney)
Fit the first of the coast masts
Wait for the crews to fit the rest
steps.waitText: the mast crews are working down the coast

steps.verb: Hand calls between the masts on a drive down the coast

name: Fibre to every mast
story: The masts are only as fast as the line behind them, and half of them run on borrowed copper. Fibre to every mast, and the phones in people's pockets get fast.
doneText: Every mast has fibre behind it. Data on the phones is fast enough that people stop noticing it, which is the point.

steps.verb: Plan the backhaul routes
Blow fibre to the nearest masts
Wait for the crews to reach the rest
steps.waitText: the crews are blowing fibre down the coast

steps.verb: Swap the copper out at the last mast
